h1: The 7 Best Printers Without Ink Subscriptions of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 printers with no ink subscription, scored on refill cost, features and fit, from Epson EcoTank tanks to Brother lasers.
summary: The Epson EcoTank ET-3850 is the best printer without an ink subscription: refillable tanks, a document feeder, Ethernet and a bonus black bottle. The ET-4800 adds fax, and the ET-2800 and ET-2400 are the cheaper tanks. The Brother lasers suit low-volume printing, and the INKvestment still uses cartridges.
intro: A subscription printer is sold cheaply and paid for monthly. The hardware discount is real, but the plan bills whether or not you print, and some versions limit which cartridges work if you cancel. A buyer who only needs a few pages a month ends up renting ink they barely use, which is the opposite of the saving that attracted them.

The cleanest escape is a printer with no plan to opt into at all. We reviewed seven models across three types, refillable ink tanks, lasers and one large-cartridge inkjet, and ranked them on how fully they avoid recurring charges, what you get for the money and who each suits. A free trial that can be ignored counts against a model far less than a plan that gates its ink.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-3850 Wireless Color All-in-One
products.verdict: Refillable tanks, an automatic document feeder and Ethernet. Office features with no ink plan.
products.description:
The Epson ET-3850 is a cartridge-free tank all-in-one with an automatic document feeder, Ethernet and wireless connectivity, scan and copy functions, and a bonus black ink bottle in the box. Refillable tanks mean you buy bottled ink when you need it, never a plan, and the bonus bottle starts you off ahead on the commonest color.

It ranks first because it bundles office features with the cleanest ink model. The ET-4800 adds fax but no bonus bottle noted, and the entry models drop the feeder.

Buy it for a home office that scans and copies multi-page documents. The caveats are a higher upfront price than the other EcoTanks and a bigger body. Skip it if you print only occasionally and want the cheapest tank printer.
cons: Higher upfront price than other EcoTanks
Bigger body than the entry models
products.idealFor: Home offices that scan and copy multi-page documents.
products.skipIf: You print only occasionally and want the cheapest tank printer.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-4800 Wireless All-in-One
products.verdict: Same subscription-free tank base with a feeder, Ethernet and a built-in fax.
products.description:
The Epson ET-4800 uses the same subscription-free tank base with an automatic document feeder, Ethernet, wireless, a built-in fax, and scan and copy functions, and no subscription program to opt into. Fax is the differentiator: it keeps a landline-style workflow alive for offices that still need it.

It ranks second because fax is niche, and no bonus ink bottle is noted. It costs less than the ET-3850, which is its argument.

Buy it for a small office that still sends occasional faxes. Skip it if you never fax and would rather save the money. Without the extra bottle, factor in the first refill sooner than on the ET-3850, and keep the bottle shelf-ready.
cons: Fax is niche for most buyers
products.idealFor: Small offices that still send occasional faxes.
products.skipIf: You never fax and would rather save the money.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One
products.verdict: The simplest way to dodge ink plans: a wireless tank printer with bottled refills.
products.description:
The Epson ET-2800 is a wireless color tank printer with print, scan and copy functions, a compact footprint, bottled ink refills and no subscription program. It is the simplest route past ink plans, and small enough for a dorm desk.

It ranks third because it has no automatic document feeder and no Ethernet port. It costs less than the larger EcoTanks, though, and it covers most home needs.

Buy it for a student or light home user who wants zero ink plans and a compact machine. Skip it if you scan multi-page documents regularly. A flatbed handles single pages without trouble, but a stack takes a long time, and you must stay at the glass for every sheet.
products.idealFor: Students and light home users who want zero ink plans.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2400 Wireless Color All-in-One
products.verdict: A step below the ET-2800 in price with the same subscription-free tank design.
products.description:
The Epson ET-2400 is a wireless color tank printer with print, scan and copy, bottled ink and no subscription, priced below the ET-2800. The design is deliberately plain, which keeps setup simple.

It ranks fourth because it is close to the ET-2800 in capability and also lacks a feeder or Ethernet. The price gap is its only real advantage.

Buy it for a family that prints every week and wants the lowest tank price. Skip it if you need a feeder or a wired network. If the ET-2800 is nearly the same cost in your market, choose it for the visible ink levels on its front panel, which help you refill before a tank runs dry.
pros: No ink subscription to opt into
cons: Close to the ET-2800 in capability
products.idealFor: Families who print every week and want the lowest tank price.
products.skipIf: You need a feeder or wired network.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: Black-and-white laser with duplex and a 250-sheet tray. Its Refresh plan is optional.
products.description:
Brother's DCP-L2640DW runs on toner rather than liquid ink, prints on both sides automatically, holds 250 sheets and offers wireless and mobile printing, with an optional Refresh subscription trial attached to the listing. Toner does not dry out, so a laser handles weeks of idle time between jobs, which suits infrequent printers who dread a clogged print head.

It ranks fifth because it prints only black and white, and the listing includes a trial offer you should ignore. It beats every inkjet on idle reliability.

Buy it if you print mostly text and print rarely. Skip it if you need color pages or photos. Standard toner works without enrolling, so you can decline the trial.
cons: Listing includes a trial offer to ignore
products.idealFor: People who print mostly text and print rarely.
products.skipIf: You need colour pages or photos.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Wireless Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: A colour laser with duplex and no bundled plan. Toner is bought only as needed.
products.description:
The Brother HL-L3220CDW is a color laser at 19 pages per minute, with automatic duplex, a 250-sheet tray and no bundled subscription in the listing. Toner is bought individually when needed, which avoids any plan.

It ranks sixth because it is print only, with no scanner, and color toner pages cost more than tank pages. It suits modest volumes.

Buy it for color reports and handouts at moderate volume. Skip it if you need scanning or copying. Compared with the tank printers, per-page color cost is higher, so it makes the most sense for lighter printing where a laser's crisp text and idle reliability matter more than cheap color pages.
products.idealFor: Colour reports and handouts at modest volumes.

products.name: Brother INKvestment MCF-J5010DW Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One
products.verdict: Big INKvestment cartridges and a touchscreen. Less subscription-free than a tank, but no plan bundled.
products.description:
The Brother INKvestment MCF-J5010DW is a color inkjet all-in-one with larger INKvestment cartridges, a 2.7 inch touchscreen, automatic two-sided printing and copy and scan, with no bundled subscription. Larger cartridges mean fewer swaps.

It ranks last because it is still a cartridge printer, so you remain exposed to cartridge pricing. It is less subscription-free than a tank printer in spirit.

Buy it if you want cartridges and an easy interface. Skip it if you want to avoid cartridge pricing entirely. The touchscreen is pleasant, but the tanks above reduce long-term costs more effectively, and cartridge replacement is a recurring expense you can avoid.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want cartridges and an easy interface.
products.skipIf: You want to avoid cartridge pricing entirely.

whatMatters.detail: A tank printer is refilled from a bottle, a cartridge printer swaps a sealed unit and a laser uses toner powder. Tanks cost the least per page, and lasers hold up best when idle. Check the product title for the words EcoTank, cartridge or laser before you order, because the ink method decides your long-term bill more than the sticker price, and the title usually says which kind it is.

Some listings include a free trial of a manufacturer subscription that can tie ink supply to a plan. An optional trial is fine, but check that regular cartridges still work without it. Look for any mention of enrollment or a monthly plan in the bullets, and read the fine print. The Brother DCP-L2640DW lists an optional trial, while the Epson tanks list none.

If you print under 100 pages a month, a laser stays ready without clogging. If you print more or in color, a tank usually costs far less per page. Estimate your monthly pages before choosing. Pick a laser for light text work, and an EcoTank when color or volume enters the picture, then check how fast you finish a bottle.

A flatbed-only printer makes scanning stacks of paper slow. An automatic document feeder and Ethernet help in a home office. Look for ADF and Ethernet in the spec bullets. The ET-3850 and ET-4800 list both a feeder and Ethernet, while the ET-2800 and ET-2400 are wireless with flatbed scanning only.

Automatic duplex saves paper on long documents. Some models in this guide include it, others do not. Check the listing for automatic 2-sided printing, not only manual duplex. The Brother lasers and the INKvestment list it, while the EcoTank entries here do not highlight it.

faq.a: A plan bills monthly whether or not you print, and some can limit which cartridges work if you cancel. A tank or laser printer lets you buy ink or toner only when you need it.

faq.q: Is the Brother Refresh Subscription mandatory?
faq.a: On the DCP-L2640DW listing it is an optional trial. Standard toner cartridges bought separately work without enrolling. Check that your listing makes the same distinction before buying, and decline the trial at setup. Doing so avoids a bill after the trial period ends.

faq.q: Is an EcoTank worth it over a cheaper cartridge printer?
faq.a: If you print more than occasionally, yes. Refillable tanks avoid cartridge pricing, and the ET-2800 or ET-2400 are priced close to many cartridge printers, so the saving starts early and grows with every refill bottle.

faq.q: Can an EcoTank dry out if I rarely print?
faq.a: Any inkjet can clog if left idle for months. Print a test page every few weeks to keep the nozzles moving. If you print rarely, a laser like the Brother DCP-L2640DW is the safer choice.

faq.q: Do I need the ADF on the ET-3850?
faq.a: Only if you scan multi-page documents. For single sheets, a flatbed model like the ET-2800 is fine. The feeder saves lifting the lid on every page, which matters on contracts and statements.

Tank printers generally cost least per color page, which is where the biggest savings appear. For black-only text at low volume, a laser can be competitive because toner does not go stale between jobs.

finalTake: The Epson ET-3850 is the right printer for anyone who wants to avoid ink plans, since tanks, a feeder and Ethernet arrive without a subscription. Choose the ET-2800 for light use and a Brother laser if you print rarely and only in black. Read every listing for trial offers.
